**Visual Analysis:**

- **Affected part:** Stem/crown area at or near soil level
- **Key features:**
  - Dense, white cottony/fluffy mycelial mat covering the tissue
  - Numerous small, round sclerotia (mustard-seed sized, ~1-2mm) scattered throughout the mycelium, initially white turning to yellowish-tan
  - Underlying plant tissue appears necrotic/rotted (brown)

**Reasoning through candidates:**

- **Southern Blight** (*Sclerotium rolfsii*): The hallmark signs are dense white cottony mycelium AND small, round, tan sclerotia (mustard-seed sized) forming at the stem base/crown. This matches perfectly.
- **Sclerotinia Timber Rot**: Also produces white mycelium and sclerotia, but sclerotia are large, irregular, and eventually turn black — not the small, round, tan ones seen here.
- **Gray Mold** (*Botrytis*): Mycelium is grayish and produces no such sclerotia.
- **Rhizopus Soft Rots**: Has fluffy mycelium but very different overall morphology and no small round sclerotia.

The small, round, mustard-seed-sized sclerotia embedded in dense white mycelium at the plant crown/stem base is the textbook signature of Southern Blight.

Sclerotinia would produce larger, irregular, eventually black sclerotia; Gray Mold lacks this sclerotial morphology entirely."}
